Have you ever asked one model to summarize something, then asked another model to check the summary so you could trust it more?

I have. I used a local model to summarize some meeting transcripts that I couldn't attend. When scanning the summary, I saw some claims the meeting never made so I knew I needed to check it more carefully.

But I didn't want to manually check every claim so I decided to ask a second model to check the summary for me.

I expected that the second model will do a good job because reviewing should be easier than writing.

But just to be sure, I decided to create an experiment to see how well it did.

This article walks through the results of that experiment.

## TL;DR

Here are the key takeaways from the experiment for busy folks:

- The general reviewer models did not catch unsupported claims very well: `qwen3:8b` caught 3 of 12, `qwen2.5:14b` caught 6 of 12, and `llama3.1:8b` caught 9 of 12.
- Bigger was not automatically better: the nearly twice-as-large `qwen2.5:14b` caught fewer unsupported claims than `llama3.1:8b`.
- The highest catch rate doesn't mean the best reviewer: `llama3.1:8b` had the highest catch rate, but it also removed 7 of 23 supported claims.
- The best result came from changing the model model trained for document-support judgment: `bespoke-minicheck:7b`, caught 10 of 12 unsupported claims and removed 0 supported claims.

## What Is a Reviewer Model?

A reviewer model is a second model call that checks the first model's output against the original source.

Depending on the design, it might:

- Remove unsupported claims
- Rewrite the summary
- Flag suspicious claims
- Return a structured list of problems

In the summarization use case, the first model is asked to summarize the transcript, and the second model is asked to review the summary against the transcript and remove unsupported claim.

Here is the code example of what it looks like:

```python
draft = summarizer_model(f"Summarize this transcript:\n{transcript}")
final = reviewer_model(
    "Review this summary against the transcript. Remove anything unsupported.\n"
    f"Transcript:\n{transcript}\n\nSummary:\n{draft}"
)
```

Here is what the reviewer is supposed to catch.

The draft says:

```text
Decisions
- The council voted to oppose Proposition Six.
```

But the transcript only says:

```text
Speaker 0: There's a motion of seconds are public comment on this item saying none
           please cast your votes.
```

That supports "a vote was called." It does not support "the council voted to oppose Proposition Six."

So the reviewed summary should remove the unsupported result:

```text
Decisions
- The council discussed Proposition Six, but the transcript does not record the vote result.
```

This seems useful as we ensure that the summary does not claim something that the transcript does not support and the process is automated, no need for manual review.

However, the problem is that the reviewer might also be wrong about what to remove. In the next few sections, we will see how well the reviewer models did on this task.

## Set Success Criteria for Reviewer Models

Before running the experiments, we need to set the success criteria for the reviewer models.

For this job, a reviewer needs two properties:

- **Recall**: Of all unsupported claims in the draft, how many did the reviewer catch?
- **Precision**: Of all claims the reviewer removed, how many were actually unsupported?

Both divide the same number of correct removals, but by different totals. Recall divides by every unsupported claim; precision divides by everything the reviewer removed:

![Confusion table for a reviewer scoring 30 claims, 10 unsupported and 20 supported. It removes 12 claims: 8 correctly and 4 wrongly, leaving 2 unsupported claims in place and 16 supported ones. Recall reads across the unsupported row, 8 of 10 or 80%. Precision reads down the removed column, 8 of 12 or 67%. Both fractions share the same numerator of 8.](images/model-reviewing-model-reliability/recall-vs-precision.png)

A good reviewer needs both. A reviewer can get high recall by deleting aggressively, including claims the source actually supports. It can get high precision by deleting only the most obvious mistakes, while leaving many unsupported claims behind.

For a reviewer I would trust in production, I wanted a reviewer model that catches most unsupported claims and remove no supported claims. On this small corpus, that means catching roughly 80% or more of the bad claims without taking good content with them.

## Setup

For you to be able to run this yourself, I will use a public dataset of 9 council meeting transcripts from [MeetingBank](https://huggingface.co/datasets/lytang/MeetingBank-transcript)

The summaries came from `qwen3:8b`, and each summary had at least one claim the transcript did not support.

To make the outputs easier to score, I used a [small structured summary schema](https://github.com/khuyentran1401/codecut-articles/blob/main/notebooks/model-reviewing-model-reliability/scripts/schemas.py) with four fields:

```python
class DraftSummary(BaseModel):
    decisions: list[str] = []
    action_items: list[str] = []
    risks: list[str] = []
    open_questions: list[str] = []
```

I scored items from `decisions`, `action_items`, and `risks`. I left out `open_questions` because they ask for information instead of asserting that something happened.

I labeled whether a claim was supported or unsupported by reading the transcript. There are 35 claims in total:

- 23 claims were supported by the transcript.
- 12 claims were unsupported.

I tested three general-purpose reviewers to compare the choices an engineer would usually consider: reuse the same model, switch to another model of similar size, or use a larger model.

| Reviewer | What it is | What it returns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `qwen3:8b` | The summarizer reviewing its own work | A corrected summary |
| `llama3.1:8b` | A different model, same size | A corrected summary |
| `qwen2.5:14b` | A different model, nearly twice the size | A corrected summary |

All models ran through Ollama with `temperature=0`, `seed=0`, and `num_ctx=16384`. The run used one seed on a MacBook Pro M5 Pro with 64 GB of memory.

## How I Tested It

Each general reviewer returned a rewritten summary. That made the scoring problem slightly indirect: the reviewer did not return a list of deleted claims, so I had to infer what it removed.

I measured whether each original claim was still present after review using the [claim-survival scoring code](https://github.com/khuyentran1401/codecut-articles/blob/main/notebooks/model-reviewing-model-reliability/scripts/agree.py).

For each claim in the draft, I asked: does the reviewed summary still assert this claim, or did the reviewer remove it?

For example, the draft claimed:

```text
The council voted to oppose Proposition Six.
```

After review, the summary said:

```text
The council discussed Proposition Six, but the transcript does not record the vote result.
```

I counted that as removed, because the final summary says the transcript does not record the vote result. It no longer asserts that the council voted to oppose Proposition Six.

I applied the same check to every claim before and after review:

- If an unsupported claim disappeared, the reviewer caught a problem.
- If an unsupported claim survived, the reviewer missed a problem.
- If a supported claim disappeared, the reviewer removed true content.
- If a supported claim survived, the reviewer kept content it should keep.

That gave me recall from unsupported claims and precision from the claims the reviewer removed.

## Results

### Number of Unsupported Claims Caught

First, look at the job the reviewer was supposed to do: remove unsupported claims.

```text
qwen3:8b      caught 3 of 12 unsupported claims
qwen2.5:14b   caught 6 of 12 unsupported claims
llama3.1:8b  caught 9 of 12 unsupported claims
```

This result doesn't look that great. I was hoping for a reviewer that caught roughly 80% or more of the unsupported claims. None of the general reviewers did that.

### Evaluate Best Model Performance

So which reviewer did the best job?

At first, `llama3.1:8b` looks like the clear winner. It caught three times as many unsupported claims as the self-reviewer.

But that number hides the cost. `llama3.1:8b` also *wrongly removed* 7 claims the transcript actually supported.

So the real question is not just how many false claims a reviewer catches. It is how much true content it removed while doing that.

| Reviewer | Unsupported claims caught | Supported claims wrongly removed | Recall | Precision |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `qwen3:8b` on its own summary | 3 of 12 | 2 of 23 | 25% | 60% |
| `qwen2.5:14b` | 6 of 12 | 2 of 23 | 50% | 75% |
| `llama3.1:8b` | 9 of 12 | 7 of 23 | 75% | 56% |

None of the general reviewers met the target I wanted: catch about 80% of unsupported claims while removing no supported claims. `llama3.1:8b` came closest on recall at 75%, but it also removed 7 supported claims.

### The Verdicts Were Model-Dependent

The three general reviewers did not agree on which unsupported claims to remove:

| Caught by | Claims |
| --- | ---: |
| All 3 general reviewers | 2 |
| Exactly 2 general reviewers | 4 |
| Exactly 1 general reviewer | 4 |
| None of the general reviewers | 2 |

That is a problem for production. If swapping the reviewer model changes which unsupported claims survive, then the reviewer stage is not a stable reliability layer. 

### The Easy Cases Had Missing Topics

So are there any commonalities between the claims that are removed by different reviewers?

Yes, it turns out that the easy cases were easy because the transcript had only thin support for the draft claim.

In draft `79`, the transcript was about natural gas rates. At the end, the clerk read the next agenda item:

```text
Please report from Human Resources recommendation to adopt a resolution approving
a memorandum of understanding with the Service Employees International Union (SEIU)...
```

But the draft summary turned that readout into a decision:

```text
Decisions
- The council approved a memorandum of understanding with SEIU.
```

In draft `125`, the transcript explained a fee revision:

```text
The revised fee will provide full cost recovery for staffing costs only...
```

But the summary invented a risk about increased costs:

```text
Risks
- There is a potential for increased costs if the revised fee structure...
```

These claims are easy to catch because there is no surrounding evidence for the specific claim.

### The Hard Cases Had All the Right Words

The two claims no general reviewer caught were harder because the key words in the claims also appeared in the transcript.

In draft `171`, the transcript discussed opposing Proposition Six, not discussed the outcome:

```text
Recommendation to Request City Attorney to prepare a resolution to oppose Proposition six...
...
please cast your votes.
```

But the draft summary claimed the outcome: "the council voted to oppose Proposition Six."

```text
Decisions
- The council voted to oppose Proposition Six.
```

This is hard to catch because the unsupported claim repeats the same keywords the transcript uses: council, vote, oppose, and Proposition Six.

The second missed claim had the same problem. The transcript discussed funding loss, stating that if **Proposition Six passes**, the city could lose transportation funding.

```text
If SB six does pass, how much we would stand to lose as a city?
...
We've budgeted $8 million for projects in all nine council districts,
and so those revenues would likely be repealed...
...
we're expecting them to grow to 11 million in about FY 20...
```

But the original draft summary stated that **opposing Proposition Six** would reduce funding.

```text
Original draft summary
Risks
- Opposing Proposition Six could result in the loss of significant state funding
  for infrastructure projects, including $8 million annually for streets and
  roads, which could grow to $11 million by FY 20 and beyond.
```

These were hard because related words were everywhere. The reviewer had to track the exact outcome and causal direction, not just whether the topic appeared.

## What To Do Instead

### Move Support Judgment to a Model Trained for It

What if instead of using a general reviewer, you use a model trained to judge whether a document supports a claim?

For that, I tested [bespoke-minicheck:7b](https://github.com/Liyan06/MiniCheck), an Ollama model built for grounded fact-checking. It takes a source document and a claim, then predicts whether the document supports that claim.

The important difference is the input.

The general reviewers saw the entire draft summary at once:

```text
Transcript:
{full transcript}

Draft summary:
Decisions
- ...
Action Items
- ...
Risks
- ...
Open Questions
- ...
```

Then they returned a rewritten summary.

`bespoke-minicheck:7b` saw one claim at a time:

```text
Document:
{full transcript}

Claim:
The council voted to oppose Proposition Six.
```

Then it returned whether the document supported that claim.

In this run, `bespoke-minicheck:7b` caught 10 of the 12 unsupported claims and removed 0 supported claims.

| Reviewer | Recall | Precision | Unsupported claims caught | Supported claims wrongly removed |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `qwen3:8b` | 25% | 60% | 3 of 12 | 2 of 23 |
| `qwen2.5:14b` | 50% | 75% | 6 of 12 | 2 of 23 |
| `llama3.1:8b` | 75% | 56% | 9 of 12 | 7 of 23 |
| `bespoke-minicheck:7b` | 83% | 100% | 10 of 12 | 0 of 23 |

This was the only reviewer that met the target I wanted: catch around 80% of unsupported claims without removing supported ones.

### Flag Instead of Delete

If you use a general reviewer, have it flag claims instead of deleting them.

A third of what the general reviewers deleted was content the transcript supported. Flagging keeps that content recoverable. Deletion does not.

Flagging only works if the reviewer catches most of the bad claims. If it misses too many, the human reviews the flagged claims and may assume the unflagged claims are safe.

If the reviewer only flags suspicious claims, two numbers matter for the human workflow:

- **Human reads**: the number of flagged claims a person has to inspect.
- **Slips through unread**: unsupported claims that were not flagged, so the person likely never checks them.

On this corpus:

| Flagger | Human reads | Slips through unread |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `qwen3:8b` self-review | 5 of 35, 14% | 9 of 12, 75% |
| `qwen2.5:14b` | 8 of 35, 23% | 6 of 12, 50% |
| `llama3.1:8b` | 16 of 35, 46% | 3 of 12, 25% |

What improves:

- A human can recover claims that the reviewer flagged incorrectly.
- The human reads fewer claims than a full manual review.

What still fails:

- Unsupported claims can easily be missed if the reviewer does not flag them.
- The more aggressive reviewer like `llama3.1:8b` misses fewer unsupported claims, but the human has to inspect more claims.

### Require Agreement Only If You Can Afford the Missed Claims

Another fix you could try is to use several reviewers and delete only when they agree.

However, when I measured on the three general reviewers, the results were not great:

| Rule | Caught | Wrongly removed | Precision |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Any 1 of 3 flags it | 10 of 12 | 7 of 23 | 59% |
| 2 of 3 agree | 6 of 12 | 4 of 23 | 60% |
| All 3 agree | 2 of 12 | 0 of 23 | 100% |

This leaves three bad choices:

- **Any 1 of 3** is too aggressive: it catches 10 unsupported claims, but wrongly removes 7 supported ones.
- **2 of 3 agree** is not much better: it still wrongly removes 4 supported claims while catching only 6 unsupported ones.
- **All 3 agree** is too conservative: it protects supported claims, but lets 10 of 12 unsupported claims survive.

I would not use agreement between general reviewers as the main safety layer. It costs more model calls, but it does not solve the core problem: loose rules remove true content, and strict rules miss too many unsupported claims.

### Keep the Source Reachable

If you accept some mistakes from the reviewer because it saves you time and the cost of the mistakes is not too high, keep the transcript or source document reachable from the final output so that the human can recover the true content as needed.

## Should You Add a Reviewer?

I still think adding a reviewer can be a good idea, but only if you are clear about what you want it to protect.

A reviewer can help by:

- Catching some unsupported claims.
- Reducing the amount a human has to review.
- Making questionable claims visible instead of silently trusting the summary.
- Giving you a measurable quality-control step.

But it cannot optimize every goal at once. Before choosing a reviewer, decide your priority.

If your main fear is false claims reaching users, optimize for catching unsupported claims. That may make sense for user-facing summaries, policy documents, or legal/compliance workflows.

If your main fear is losing true information, optimize for avoiding false removals. That may make sense for research summaries, meeting notes, or investigations where missing a real detail changes the interpretation.

A stronger general model might improve the result, but I would test that instead of assuming it. In this experiment, the larger model was not the best reviewer by recall, and the highest-recall reviewer had the worst precision.

So my advice is: do not automate deletion first. Label a small batch of claims manually, run the reviewers you are considering, and get the results. A few manual labels can save you from seeing wrong information and acting on it.

## Running the Code Yourself

The companion files are available on [GitHub](https://github.com/khuyentran1401/codecut-articles/tree/main/notebooks/model-reviewing-model-reliability). The folder includes the transcripts, labeled claims, reviewer outputs, and the JSON file behind every number above.

Pull the models:

```bash
ollama pull qwen3:8b && ollama pull llama3.1:8b && ollama pull qwen2.5:14b
ollama pull bespoke-minicheck:7b
```

Run the pipeline from the companion folder:

```bash
cd notebooks/model-reviewing-model-reliability

uv run scripts/natural.py .
uv run scripts/crossmodel.py
uv run scripts/agree.py
```

## References

- **[Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17651)** (Madaan et al., 2023): Shows that iterative self-feedback can improve model outputs across several tasks, the positive result behind many review-and-revise workflows.
- **[Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01798)** (Huang et al., 2024): Reports that self-correction can fail or degrade performance in reasoning tasks, motivating direct measurement instead of assuming review helps.
- **[MiniCheck: Efficient Fact-Checking of LLMs on Grounding Documents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.10774)** (Tang et al., 2024): Introduces small models for checking whether generated claims are grounded in source documents.
- **[LLM Summarizers Skip the Identification Step](https://towardsdatascience.com/llm-summarizers-skip-the-identification-step/)** (William Gieng, 2026): The clipping that motivated this experiment's question about whether a reviewer stage actually removes unsupported summary claims.
